I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
control eating strictly to feel in control

Threat.value: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening

Memory.value: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt

Negative Appraisals.value: I used to be a happy person but now I am always miserable.
I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

issues.item: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Verbal Access' conflicts with the other memory items. Being able to talk about the rape very easily is hard to reconcile with a profile centered on fragmented, unreal, image-based trauma memory and severe PTSD symptoms.

issues.item: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me.
issues.explanation: Within the Memory node, 'Story Feels Unreal' and 'Snapshot Memory' suggest poorly elaborated, emotionally overwhelming trauma memory, which clashes with 'Verbal Access'. This makes the Memory node internally inconsistent.

issues.item: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: 'Physical Vulnerability' is less coherent with the rest of the profile because the dominant appraisals are global loss and mistrust, while the reported threat pattern is generalized anticipatory danger rather than fear specifically tied to bodily injury. For rape it is possible, but here it is the least well integrated appraisal relative to the other selected items.

vignette:
Elena, a 47-year-old social ministry worker who had spent two decades comforting others in crisis, could no longer step inside her own church. The rape had happened three years ago, after she stayed late to prepare meal packages for a homeless shelter. A man she had tried to help-someone she had prayed with, shared coffee with-followed her into the storage room. What she remembered now was not a sequence but a series of frozen images, like slides in a projector that would not stop: the fluorescent light flickering above her, the grain of the concrete floor against her cheek, the silver buckle of his belt catching the light. She could see these moments with perfect clarity, but when her therapist asked her to describe what had happened next, Elena's mouth went dry. She knew what came after the buckle, knew it in her bones and in the way her stomach clenched every night at dusk, but the words would not come. They felt stuck somewhere behind her breastbone, too heavy and too sharp to push past her lips.

In the months that followed, Elena had come to believe that she had lost something essential about herself. She used to be the person who laughed easily, who hummed while she folded laundry, who could sit in silence with a grieving parishioner and feel a quiet peace. Now she was certain that happiness had been stolen from her permanently, and worse, that she deserved to suffer. When she caught herself almost smiling at a child's joke, she would immediately think of the assault and remind herself that she had no right to feel joy. She had begun to punish herself in small, deliberate ways: skipping meals, refusing to let herself sit down during the day, standing instead of resting. Eating had become a matter of strict control-she measured every portion, counted every bite, because the discipline of hunger made her feel, for a few hours, that she was managing something in a life that had spun out of her control.

Her husband, Carlos, had tried to understand. He held her when she woke gasping from nightmares, made her tea, asked gentle questions. But Elena had stopped being able to look at him without feeling a wave of shame so deep it made her nauseous. She felt that what had happened to her body had marked it somehow, made it something to be hidden and despised. Physical intimacy had ended within weeks of the assault. When Carlos reached for her hand in the car, she would flinch and pretend she had not noticed. She had come to believe that her body was no longer hers to share-that it had been violated and dirtied, and that anyone who touched her would somehow feel the stain.

Her work had become a minefield. The church office was quiet in the afternoons, and that silence now felt like the moment before a trap springs. Elena would find herself holding her breath, listening for footsteps, her heart hammering until she had to leave her desk and walk outside. If a meeting ran late or a delivery truck did not arrive on time, she immediately assumed that something terrible had happened-that Carlos had been in an accident, that her mother had fallen, that the world was about to collapse again. She could not relax, even at home with the doors locked and her dog at her feet. Her body stayed braced, muscles tight, waiting for the next blow.

What finally brought Elena to a therapist's office was not her own suffering, but a moment at work when a young woman came to her for comfort after a sexual assault. Elena had sat across from her, unable to speak, unable to pray, unable to do anything but see the concrete floor and the flickering light. She had excused herself, gone to the bathroom, and vomited. The next day, she called the clinic. She was terrified of what therapy might demand of her-afraid that finding words would break her open, afraid that letting go of her vigilance would invite danger, afraid that if she stopped punishing herself, she would be betraying some unspoken rule of survival. But she was also, beneath the fear, desperately hoping that the woman she used to be was not gone forever.
